content: Repetin is an extracellular matrix protein that is expressed in the epidermis. In humans, it is encoded by the RPTN gene. This protein belongs to the S100 fused-type protein family and contains an EF-hand structural domain, which is a helix-loop-helix motif involved in calcium binding. Repetin plays a critical role in the formation of the cornified cell envelope, a structure essential for the barrier function of the skin. It is a multifunctional epidermal matrix protein with diverse roles in skin physiology. The RPTN protein has the ability to reversibly bind calcium, which is important for its function. The RPTN gene spans 5,634 base pairs in length. It is located on the minus strand of the genome, starting at 152,126,071 base pairs from the pter (short arm of the chromosome) and ending at 152,131,704 base pairs from the pter. RPTN is one of the genes that exhibit differences between modern humans and Neanderthals. This protein contributes to the protection of skin cells. The absence of this protein in Neanderthals may have made them better adapted to cold climates but less equipped to handle certain diseases. RPTN is one of 30 specific genetic differences identified between the DNA of present-day humans and that of Neanderthals.
